text:
What I love about this and what intrigues me at the same time is how biology and a part of the evolutionary theory is expressed very clearly in this real life situation.

The Tekken world of Pakistan was separated from the outside Tekken world; very few things, like information and news, got in or got out of the country. Because of this, the Pakistani community developed a style of playing Tekken that was completely different from those in the outside world. Playstyle like the NA playstyle or the Japanese/Korean playstyle are dominant, and for the most part, very common. And because of this separation and this boundary, those within Pakistan shocked the world.

I love this story and would wish Arslan the very best in all things.

This reminds me of something from the very dim and distant esports past, nearly 20 years ago. In August 2000, Barrysworld held a European Cup for 4v4 Quake3 TDM and Russia had qualified from what was assumed to be a fairly weak CIS nation group.

The Russian scene was totally unknown, and the Russian team hardly spoke any English. This wasn't the only strange thing, they played with a particularly strange style. They had keyboards on their laps, and the mouse directly in front of them, apparently due to the cramped conditions they mostly played in at Moscow Cybercafes.

They also had visa issues getting to London for the tournament, only finally being granted the visas a few days before the tournament.

And they beat everyone. Hard.

author: user_1f7c6317
text:
You guys have no clue what this does to my heart. I'm so happy & a  little sad (for myself, and those who were around me). I lived in Pakistan for 10 years, even the same city as Arslan (A.I. Town reprazent!)  I met some of the best FG gamers in my life here, I learnt from them, I shared with them. We were a KoF crew but I was the Tekken guy (3 to be exact). Like Arslan, all we could do was imagine going outside of the country to represent ourselves. To show the world "look, for all the shitty things we're known for, we're good at *this*! Give us a chance to prove ourselves!" but unlike Arslan we'd just talk about it. Some dreams remain dreams, right?   

We did try though, we had local tournaments, tried to figure out the whole online thing, entered competitions in odd international places and Win (but couldn't get recognition outside of  developers pats on the back and subtle nods like having a player character's name changed to one of ours or having the player's name graffitied on the stage background).  That was over 20 years ago, our last attempt to leave our mark was this Combo Music Video from 2005 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vzrtN-8trRY - we were RKZ KOF).  Then, we drifted apart, life got in the way, some got married, some moved abroad...some lived a short life. All I have left are these memories. But to see you up there, acknowledged and accepted, to have someone talk of a "Pakistani Style", to have people FLY to Pakistan to learn it, to have you as a catalyst...  I guess what I'm trying to say is: From all us old heads who tried and failed,  all the unsung who the world never knew of: Thank you.  You did what could not and        We live through you my friend, May your Dream Match Never End.

author: user_a9c08753
text: Arslan is a common first name in Pakistan. It means "Lion" in Urdu (The main language spoken in Pakistan), Turkish and I think also in Persian. So no, it's not a reference to some anime. It's a name being used for thousands of years in this region. I know that in western media this name was taken and slightly changed into "Aslan" and was used in a series of Books and Movies called "Narnia", where they named a lion character Aslan. That is probably what made the the slightly modified version popular over there. And subsequently in Japan as well.
